paragraphs: So he had to drive at full speed, and he had no money for horses. He had forty kopecks, and that was all, all that was left after so many years of prosperity! But at home he had an old silver watch that had stopped working long ago. He snatched it up and took it to a Jewish watchmaker who had a shop in the market-place. The Jew gave him six roubles for it.

“I didn’t even expect that much!” cried Mitya, ecstatic. (He was still in a state of ecstasy.) He grabbed his six roubles and ran home. At home he borrowed three roubles from the people of the house. They were so fond of him that they gladly gave it, though it was all they had. In his excitement Mitya told them on the spot that his fate would be decided that day. In desperate haste he described the whole scheme he had put before Samsonov, Samsonov’s decision, his own hopes for the future, and so on. These people had been told many of their lodger’s secrets before, so they thought of him as a gentleman who was not at all proud, and almost one of themselves. With nine roubles collected, Mitya sent for posting-horses to take him to the Volovya station. This is how it came to be remembered and established that “at midday, on the day before the event, Mitya had not a farthing, and that he had sold his watch to get money and had borrowed three roubles from his landlord, all in the presence of witnesses.”
I note this fact now. Later it will be clear why I do.

He was radiant with joyful hope that he would at last solve all his difficulties. Yet as he drew near Volovya station, he trembled at the thought of what Grushenka might be doing while he was away. What if she made up her mind today to go to Fyodor Pavlovitch? That was why he had gone off without telling her, and why he had told his landlady not to say where he had gone, if anyone came asking for him.

“I must get back tonight, I must,” he kept repeating as he was jolted along in the cart. “And I expect I’ll have to bring this Lyagavy back here with me ... to draw up the deed.” So Mitya mused, with a throbbing heart. But alas! His dreams were not fated to come true.

To begin with, he was late. He took a short cut from Volovya station that turned out to be eighteen versts instead of twelve. Second, he did not find the priest at home at Ilyinskoe, because he had gone off to a neighboring village. Mitya set off there with the same exhausted horses, and by the time he found the priest it was almost dark.

The priest was a shy, amiable-looking little man. He told Mitya at once that Lyagavy had stayed with him at first, but was now at Suhoy Possyolok, spending the night in the forester’s cottage, since he was buying timber there too. Mitya urgently begged him to take him to Lyagavy at once and so “save him, so to speak.” After some hesitation the priest agreed to lead him to Suhoy Possyolok. His curiosity was obviously aroused. But unluckily he suggested going on foot, since it was not “much over” a verst. Mitya agreed, of course, and marched off with his yard-long strides, so that the poor priest almost had to run after him. He was a very cautious man, though not old.

Mitya began talking to him at once about his plans, too. Nervous and excited, he asked advice about Lyagavy and talked all the way. The priest listened attentively but gave little advice. He turned off Mitya’s questions with: “I don’t know. Ah, I can’t say. How can I tell?” and so on. When Mitya began to speak of his quarrel with his father over his inheritance, the priest was positively alarmed, since he was dependent on Fyodor Pavlovitch in some way. He did ask, with surprise, why Mitya called the peasant-trader Gorstkin by the name Lyagavy. He kindly explained that although the man’s name really was Lyagavy, he was never called that, because he would be badly offended by it. Mitya must be sure to call him Gorstkin, “or you’ll do nothing with him; he won’t even listen to you,” the priest finished.

Mitya was a little surprised for a moment, and explained that Samsonov had called him that. On hearing this, the priest dropped the subject. He would have done well to put into words his doubt: if Samsonov had sent Mitya to that peasant and called him Lyagavy, was there not something wrong about it? Was he making fun of Mitya? But Mitya had no time to stop over such trifles. He hurried on, striding along, and only when he reached Suhoy Possyolok did he realize that they had come not one verst, nor one and a half, but at least three. This annoyed him, but he controlled himself.

They went into the hut. The forester lived in one half of it, and Gorstkin was lodging in the other half, the better room, across the passage. They went into that room and lit a tallow candle. The hut was extremely overheated. On the table there was a samovar that had gone out, a tray with cups, an empty rum bottle, a bottle of vodka partly full, and some half-eaten crusts of wheaten bread. The visitor himself lay stretched out at full length on the bench, with his coat crushed up under his head for a pillow, snoring heavily. Mitya stood there, perplexed.

“Of course I must wake him. My business is too important. I’ve come in such a rush. I’m in a hurry to get back today,” he said, in great agitation. But the priest and the forester stood in silence and gave no opinion. Mitya went up and tried to wake him himself. He tried hard, but the sleeper did not wake.

“He’s drunk,” Mitya decided. “Good Lord! What am I to do? What am I to do?” And, terribly impatient, he began pulling him by the arms and by the legs, shaking his head, lifting him up and making him sit on the bench. Yet after long exertions, all he could get out of the drunken man was absurd grunts and violent but muffled oaths.
“No, you’d better wait a little,” the priest said at last, “because he’s obviously not in a fit state.”
“He’s been drinking the whole day,” the forester chimed in.
“Good heavens!” cried Mitya. “If only you knew how important this is to me and how desperate I am!”
“No, you’d better wait till morning,” the priest repeated.
“Till morning? Mercy! That’s impossible!”
And in his despair he was about to attack the sleeping man again, but stopped short at once, seeing how useless it was. The priest said nothing, and the sleepy forester looked gloomy.

“What terrible tragedies real life dreams up for people,” said Mitya, in complete despair. Sweat was streaming down his face. The priest took the moment to point out, very reasonably, that even if Mitya did manage to wake the man, he would still be drunk and unable to hold a conversation. “And your business is important,” he said, “so you’d certainly better put it off till morning.” With a gesture of despair Mitya agreed.

“Father, I will stay here with a light, and seize the favorable moment. As soon as he wakes I’ll begin. I’ll pay you for the light,” he said to the forester, “and for the night’s lodging too. You’ll remember Dmitri Karamazov. Only, Father, I don’t know what we’re to do with you. Where will you sleep?”
“No, I’m going home. I’ll take his horse and get home,” he said, pointing to the forester. “And now I’ll say good-bye. I wish you every success.”

So it was settled. The priest rode off on the forester’s horse, delighted to escape. Still, he shook his head uneasily, wondering whether he ought to tell his benefactor Fyodor Pavlovitch about this curious incident next day, “or he may hear of it at an unlucky moment, get angry, and withdraw his favor.”

The forester, scratching himself, went back to his room without a word, and Mitya sat on the bench to “catch the favorable moment,” as he put it. A deep dejection hung about his soul like a heavy mist. A profound, intense dejection! He sat thinking, but could reach no conclusion. The candle burned dimly, a cricket chirped, and the overheated room became unbearably close. Suddenly he pictured the garden, the path behind the garden, the door of his father’s house mysteriously opening and Grushenka running in. He leapt up from the bench.

“It’s a tragedy!” he said, grinding his teeth. Mechanically he went up to the sleeping man and looked at his face. He was a lean, middle-aged peasant with a very long face, flaxen curls, and a long, thin, reddish beard. He wore a blue cotton shirt and a black waistcoat, and the chain of a silver watch peeped from its pocket. Mitya looked at his face with intense hatred, and for some unknown reason the curly hair irritated him most of all.

What was unbearably humiliating was this: he had left matters of such importance and made such sacrifices, and now he, Mitya, utterly worn out, with business of such urgency, was standing over this dolt on whom his whole fate depended. And the dolt snored as though nothing were the matter, as though he had dropped from another planet.

“Oh, the irony of fate!” cried Mitya. Quite losing his head, he fell again to rousing the tipsy peasant. He roused him with a sort of ferocity. He pulled at him, pushed him, even beat him. But after five minutes of useless effort, he went back to his bench in helpless despair and sat down.

“Stupid! Stupid!” cried Mitya. “And how dishonorable it all is!” something made him add. His head began to ache horribly. “Should he fling it up and go away altogether?” he wondered. “No, wait till tomorrow now. I’ll stay on purpose. What else did I come for? Besides, I’ve no way to leave. How am I to get away from here now? Oh, the idiocy of it!”

But his head ached more and more. He sat without moving, and without realizing it he dozed off and fell asleep sitting there. He seemed to have slept for two hours or more. He was woken by his head aching so unbearably that he could have screamed. There was a hammering in his temples, and the top of his head ached. It was a long time before he was fully awake and understood what had happened to him.

At last he realized that the room was full of charcoal fumes from the stove and that he might suffocate. And the drunken peasant still lay snoring. The candle guttered and was about to go out. Mitya cried out and ran staggering across the passage into the forester’s room. The forester woke at once. But when he heard that the other room was full of fumes, he accepted it with strange unconcern, though he did go to see to it. This surprised and annoyed Mitya.
“But he’s dead, he’s dead! and ... what am I to do then?” cried Mitya frantically.

They threw open the doors and opened a window and the chimney. Mitya brought a pail of water from the passage. First he wet his own head. Then he found some rag, dipped it in the water, and put it on Lyagavy’s head. The forester still treated the matter with contempt, and when he opened the window he said grumpily:
“It’ll be all right now.”

He went back to sleep, leaving Mitya a lighted lantern. Mitya fussed over the drunken peasant for half an hour, wetting his head, and solemnly resolved not to sleep all night. But he was so worn out that when he sat down for a moment to catch his breath, he closed his eyes. Without meaning to, he stretched out full length on the bench and slept like the dead.

It was dreadfully late when he woke. It was somewhere about nine o’clock. The sun was shining brightly through the two little windows of the hut. The curly-headed peasant was sitting on the bench with his coat on. In front of him were another samovar and another bottle. Yesterday’s bottle had already been finished, and the new one was more than half empty. Mitya jumped up and saw at once that the cursed peasant was drunk again, hopelessly and incurably. He stared at him for a moment with wide-open eyes. The peasant was watching him silently and slyly, with insulting calm and even a sort of contemptuous condescension, so Mitya thought. He rushed up to him.
“Excuse me, you see ... I ... you’ve most likely heard from the forester here in the hut. I’m Lieutenant Dmitri Karamazov, the son of the old Karamazov whose copse you are buying.”
“That’s a lie!” said the peasant, calmly and confidently.
“A lie? You know Fyodor Pavlovitch?”
“I don’t know any of your Fyodor Pavlovitches,” said the peasant, speaking thickly.

“You’re bargaining with him for the copse, for the copse. Do wake up, and pull yourself together. Father Pavel of Ilyinskoe brought me here. You wrote to Samsonov, and he has sent me to you,” Mitya gasped breathlessly.
“You’re l-lying!” Lyagavy blurted out again. Mitya’s legs went cold.
“For mercy’s sake! It isn’t a joke! Maybe you’re drunk. Yet you can speak and understand ... or else ... I understand nothing!”
“You’re a painter!”
“For mercy’s sake! I’m Karamazov, Dmitri Karamazov. I have an offer to make you, an advantageous offer ... a very advantageous offer, about the copse!”
The peasant stroked his beard importantly.
“No, you’ve contracted for the job and turned out a scamp. You’re a scoundrel!”
“I assure you you’re mistaken,” cried Mitya, wringing his hands in despair. The peasant went on stroking his beard, and suddenly screwed up his eyes cunningly.
“No, you show me this: you tell me the law that allows roguery. D’you hear? You’re a scoundrel! Do you understand that?”

Mitya stepped back gloomily, and suddenly “something seemed to hit him on the head,” as he said afterwards. In an instant a light seemed to dawn in his mind, “a light was kindled and I grasped it all.” He stood there stupefied. How could he, after all a man of intelligence, have given in to such folly, been led into such an adventure, and kept it up for almost twenty-four hours, fussing around this Lyagavy, wetting his head?
“Why, the man’s drunk, dead drunk, and he’ll go on drinking now for a week. What’s the use of waiting here? And what if Samsonov sent me here on purpose? What if she—? Oh, God, what have I done?”

The peasant sat watching him and grinning. At another time Mitya might have killed the fool in a fury, but now he felt as weak as a child. He went quietly to the bench, took up his overcoat, put it on without a word, and went out of the hut. He did not find the forester in the next room. There was no one there. He took fifty kopecks in small change out of his pocket and put them on the table for his night’s lodging, the candle, and the trouble he had caused. Coming out of the hut, he saw nothing but forest all around. He walked at random, not knowing which way to turn, right or left. Hurrying there the evening before with the priest, he had not noticed the road. In his heart he felt no desire for revenge on anybody, not even on Samsonov. He strode along a narrow forest path, aimless and dazed, without noticing where he was going. A child could have knocked him down, so weak was he in body and soul. Somehow he got out of the forest, however, and a view of fields, bare after the harvest, stretched as far as the eye could see.
“What despair! What death all around!” he repeated, striding on and on.

He was saved by meeting an old merchant who was being driven across country in a hired trap. When Mitya overtook him, he asked the way, and it turned out that the old merchant was going to Volovya too. After some discussion Mitya got into the trap. Three hours later they arrived. At Volovya, Mitya ordered posting-horses at once to drive to the town, and suddenly realized that he was terribly hungry. While the horses were being harnessed, an omelette was made for him. He ate it all in an instant, ate a huge hunk of bread, ate a sausage, and swallowed three glasses of vodka. After eating, his spirits and his heart grew lighter. He flew toward the town, urged on the driver, and suddenly made a new and “unalterable” plan to get that “accursed money” before evening. “And to think, only to think that a man’s life should be ruined for the sake of that paltry three thousand!” he cried, contemptuously. “I’ll settle it today.” And if it had not been for the thought of Grushenka and of what might have happened to her, which never left him, he might have become quite cheerful again.... But the thought of her stabbed him to the heart every moment, like a sharp knife.
At last they arrived, and Mitya ran straight to Grushenka.
